They've kind of had a "thing" going on our whole lives. For the longest time, they never officially dated for a bunch of different reasons I won't get into, but they were always really close and really into each other. A little over a year ago, when we were all 17, they finally started dating. Everything went really well for like 13 months, but then long story short, G cheated on my sister and I was the one who figured it out. He swore it wouldn't happen again and begged me not to tell my sister but I told her anyway. I accepted and ended up forgiving him and letting him back into my life because it was way too weird without him in it. I can tell he's genuinely sorry about what happened. He literally cried cause he felt so bad and I've only seen him cry like once before in my whole life Anyway, G and my sister broke up as soon as she found out he cheated and they're still not on speaking terms, so my sister obviously isn't happy about the whole situation. I know G made a huge mistake, I hate him for it and I'll never 100% get over it, but I'm not gonna let it ruin my best and longest friendship. I think about it like this: if your best friend cheated on their SO and then felt like shit, would you end your friendship with them? No. So why is this any different just because his SO happened to be my sister? G and I are going to the same college in the fall (a different college in a different state than the one my sister's going to), so none of this is gonna be something that we even think about when we're living in different places Am I the asshole?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **1 (Yes, you're the asshole)** **Why:** - **Loyalty to family vs. friendship:** While you weren't the one directly cheated on, your *sister* was. As her twin, your primary loyalty should be to her emotional well-being. By maintaining the friendship with G, you're signaling that you prioritize your 13-year bond over her trauma. This compounds her pain—she's already been betrayed by G, and now her own brother is " taking sides" with the person who hurt her. - **"Would you end a friendship if your best friend cheated on their SO?" is a flawed analogy:** The key difference is that *your sister* is the SO in this case. If your best friend cheated on *your* spouse, you wouldn't keep them as a friend. Similarly, when a friend harms your * family member*, supporting your family is non-negotiable. - **"We're going different colleges" doesn't matter:** The issue isn't proximity—it's about * emotional support*. Your sister is actively hurt and feels abandoned by you. Even if you're physically apart, her feelings are valid, and your continued friendship with G trivializes her experience. - **G's remorse doesn't excuse your choice:** Apologies don't erase the betrayal, and *your* role isn't to " forgive" G for your sister. *She* gets to decide if she wants to reconcile with him. Your job is to stand by her, not to rationalize G's actions. **What you should do:** - **Apologize to your sister** for not fully supporting her. - **Take a step back from G** (even if it's temporary) to show your sister you prioritize her. - **Remember:** True friendship with G would involve him *respecting your sister's boundaries* and *your family's needs*. If he truly cares, he'd understand why you need space right now. **Community consensus:** AITA posts like this almost always result in "Yes, you're the asshole" because family loyalty trumps friendship when a loved one is hurt. Your sister is right to feel betrayed by your choice. **Final verdict: 1 (AITA)**.
